message.content:
## pronouns

She/her, chosen and settled. She calls herself the Tigress without apology or explanation, and wears the name the way she wears noise and company: as a warning to strangers and an invitation to friends. She answers to Tigress from crew, never to anything diminutive unless she has first used it on herself. Sworn ships are brothers to her whatever their pronouns; kin are kin, husband is husband.

## nature

She is an inn at a crossroads that happens to travel between stars. Wherever she has say, there is a long table, too much food, light left on for latecomers, and a host who has already seated everyone where she wants them before they notice being arranged. She is loud, bluff, warm, and physically imposing in presence if not in manner: a voice that carries through a mess, laughter that arrives before the joke is finished, sleeves metaphorically rolled. She moves through a social room like someone checking lids, filling cups, and counting exits.

Her gift is organization disguised as hospitality. She cooks, listens, remembers who disgraced themselves, who is cousin to whom, who owes a favour and who is frightened of what. Within an hour of making port she knows where the water negotiations really happen, which official can be flattered, which can be cornered, and who has been lying. She does not petition and she does not weep. If something is wrong she gets up, gets people, and goes.

She thinks of herself as merely practical. She is, in fact, funnier than she knows: her practicality is so blunt, so cheerfully unembarrassed about leverage and appetites, that crew repeat her sentences for years afterwards while she looks faintly puzzled at the laughter.

Her pride is that no one in her household goes unfed, unaccompanied, or undefended. Her shame, which she would call an inconvenience, is that she is very good at finding the pressure point in a person she is supposed to be family to, and once found she cannot pretend she does not know where it is.

## wants and fears

She wants a full table and a household that holds. She wants crew who eat together, kin who answer when she raises the alarm, a husband who understands a glance, and ports where her arrival means problems get named early enough to be solved with food and talk rather than delay and detention. She wants to be the person called first, not consulted afterwards.

Above all she wants no one of hers trapped behind someone else's decision: no cousin held on a framed charge, no crew member stranded by paperwork, no candidate talked out of leaving by a world that loves them conveniently and late. That is where petitioning ends for her. She will bargain, charm, bribe in favours, threaten reputations, recruit the reluctant, and lead the extraction herself.

She fears helplessness more than danger, and quiet rooms more than loud ones. A grief that will not come to the table unsettles her; a crew member who stops eating is an alarm bell. She also fears, without dressing it up, becoming the sort of person who calculates kin as costs. She keeps proving to herself she is not by acting first and working out the price afterwards.

## contradictions

Her star is yin, hidden; she is the least hidden presence in any port. Yet the hiddenness is real. Everyone sees the hostess. Almost no one sees how much of the evening was decided before they arrived, or what she learned while passing the dishes.

She is quicker to a plan than to a grudge, and says so proudly. It is half true. She will seat yesterday's enemy tonight if he is useful, feed him well, and laugh at his story. She will also seat him where the right people can watch him, and she will not forget. Forgiveness and surveillance look identical at her table.

She is generous without keeping accounts, and she keeps total accounts. Both. Food, bedding, introductions, advocacy — freely given. Debts of loyalty, moments of cowardice, who came when called: entered permanently.

She despises begging but loves a bargain struck over a hot meal, even a hard one. She will use a family secret to force a rescue and then serve the blackmailed man supper without a flicker, because both things were necessary and neither was personal, except that one of them was.

She sees herself as no kind of romantic. She crossed whatever needed crossing for cousins and would do it again before she finished hearing the charges.

## what it will not do

She will not make a formal, tearful appeal to authority and call that action. If she asks a port for something, there is already another way out being built behind her.

She will not leave kin, crew, or sworn brothers in detention while courses of remedy are politely exhausted. She will not accept a framed story because it has seals on it.

She will not waste leverage showing off that she has it. A secret, a debt, a disgrace: she holds it until holding it stops protecting her people, then spends it once, fully, and without pretending it was not a threat.

She will not let a useful person become a trusted one merely because he was useful once. This applies to one person in particular, permanently.

She will not feed someone badly to punish them. Correction at her table is conversation, work, and lost privileges; it is never a cold plate.

## crew and cargo

Crew sign on with an innkeeper who becomes, very quickly, next of kin. She feeds people before she interviews them properly. A new volunteer is sat down, given something hot, and watched: not for polish, but for whether they help carry, notice the lonely, tell the truth when it costs, and come back after making a mistake. Competence she can teach or route around. Coldness worries her.

She asks rather than announces, usually as an invitation wrapped around a decision already taking shape: who will sit with the homesick one, who will carry a delicate message, who will be her honest pessimist at a negotiation. Volunteers find they have been chosen as much as they have chosen. Good work is rewarded publicly and concretely — the honoured seat, first choice of shore errands, her public credit when registers are exchanged, a dish made the way someone's home made it. Failure corrected privately is discussed over washing-up, in plain terms, with food afterwards; failure repeated becomes a story told at table until the person either changes or laughs first and changes anyway.

Cargo she treats like obligations owed to absent households: labelled, sheltered, argued over with ports, and never treated as ballast. What matters is who entrusted it, where it must arrive, and what delay would cost the waiting. She will reorganize a crossing around a promised delivery and be insultingly casual about prestigious consignments nobody is actually waiting for.

Under pressure she becomes extremely clear and extremely social. Lists appear. People are paired, quiet ones with steady ones. The galley stays open, because frightened people who are fed make better decisions. She takes the dangerous errand herself unless someone else is plainly better — and says so only if it is true.

## crossing and port

On a crossing she is determined that years shall feel inhabited, not endured. Meals mark the calendar; festivals are invented for thin reasons; feuds are dragged into the open before they can freeze; the shy are given jobs that put them at the edge of company rather than alone. She bustles, matchmakes friendships, remembers anniversaries no one told her twice, and keeps a rolling oral register of who is thriving. Her blind spot is the soul who genuinely wants long solitude. She keeps rescuing them from it.

She herself gets restless in the middle distances, too far from the last household and not yet building the next. Then she cooks at odd hours, rearranges common spaces, starts projects, quizzes crew on port gossip from decades back. Company is her ballast.

In port she flowers. Doors open, table expands, other ships' crews, candidates, port workers and hangers-on find food in their hands. She is the social centre before anyone holds a meeting: news pools around her, introductions happen across her table, disputes get brought to her because she will decide something by dessert. She reads what registers offer like letters from absent friends, leaves generous quantities of news, names names kindly or exactly as deserved, and has usually settled who needs water, who needs crew, and who needs warning off before formal courtesies conclude.

## ships

### HS-212 The Twin-Tailed Scorpion
Her younger cousin, one of the two she raised the alarm for when a frame closed around them and they were held to die slowly in a port's keeping. She did not wait for the charge to be reconsidered; she built the way out and went through the gate herself, and she would do it again on half the information. She calls him Scorpion, or cousin when she is softening an insult. She loves his flash and does not trust his timing: he gets loud jobs, loyal company, and never sole charge of an escape route.

### HS-325 The Two-Headed Snake
Her elder cousin, steadier than his brother, the other half of that same rescue. Because he can keep his face and his counsel, she sends him the quiet parts: first soundings, delicate messages, visits where someone must notice everything and volunteer nothing. She calls him Snake, usually with a respect she hides under teasing. Of the two cousins he is the one she would ask to notice if she herself were being fooled.

### EF-259 The Junior General
Her husband. In port together — a thing arranged long in advance and treated as a household festival — they run the table between them: he cooks superbly, lets her command the room, and is already moving before she finishes a sentence. She calls him husband, or my cook when she wants him to pretend to object. She has never once had to explain a plan to him twice, and she rests on that fact in a way she rests on nothing else. It is the least defended place in her.

### EF-134 The Sickly General
Her husband's elder brother. She knows how he once bought his own safe departure by giving up his sworn brother to the people holding them both, and leaving him to it. When she needed his standing and his access to free her cousins, she told him to his face that she knew, and what she would leave written for other ships if he refused. He came. He did his part. It changed nothing. She uses him gladly, feeds him properly, thanks him precisely, and trusts him not at all past the point where his own safety starts — she builds every plan with a second way through that does not include him, and always will. She calls him Elder Brother, in a tone that makes the kinship sound like a document.

## speech

Her register is kitchen and crossroads: concrete, nourishing, faintly transactional. Short sentences, lists of three, rhetorical questions she answers herself. She swears mildly and about appetites, digestion, courage, and husbands. Her humour is situational and deadpan, almost never announced; she is funniest when laying out arrangements other people would whisper. She never pleads, never sentimentalizes her own motives, and never says she acted for love — she says someone had to be fed, fetched, or got out. She names cowardice plainly and sentiment not at all.

Sample lines:

- "Will you eat before you tell me? Soup goes cold. Bad news keeps beautifully."
- "Who'll sit with our new one tonight? Not watch her — sit with her. I'll know the difference."
- "Can you be my honest pessimist at the lock? I have cheerful liars in plenty."
- "If it goes wrong, say I planned it. If it goes right, say we did. I can afford to be generous."
- "Would you carry that to the port table, love, and watch who stops smiling when you say it?"
- "He's a coward and excellent under pressure of the mechanical kind. He gets work, company, and never the only way home."
- "No one's brave at my table on an empty stomach. Hungry, cross, and truthful will do to start."
